variables.name: did_start_beacon_steps
variables.description: Set when Wren starts work at the Beacon Steps. If true, she learned how wind actually moves across the ridge by testing one lantern in the worst spot, which later helps when she needs to close the gappy ninety-pace stretch or give her last lanterns to the sheepfold turn.

variables.name: did_start_sheepfold_turn
variables.description: Set when Wren starts work at the Sheepfold Turn. If true, she learned the village's forgotten fuel caches from Mr Ovens, which later helps when she needs to borrow or ration paraffin.

variables.name: did_knock_doors_that
variables.description: Set when Wren knocks on doors that used to say yes. If true, she found old Mrs Kitto and brought her back into the lantern rota, which later helps when she needs to let the village finish the job or ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.

nodes.body: The shed behind the village hall smelled of oil and wet rope. Eighty paper lanterns sat in wooden crates. They were red, gold, and pale yellow. A coil of fence wire lay on the floor next to a clipboard on a nail. Someone had written THE LIST on the top in black marker. Outside, the path up the ridge went into low cloud. The church clock said quarter past two.

choices.label: Take the list and pick a section.

nodes.body: Mrs Trewin sat on an upturned crate with her wrist strapped in a bandage, reading the list aloud. Half of it was already wrong. The Hunters had moved away two winters ago. The paraffin was not where the page said. The path above the landslip had been rerouted in February, but the margin still showed the old line as if the hill had never moved. The walking party would come down off the moor at half past five. There were three sections and one afternoon for all of them.

choices.label: Start at the Beacon Steps.
Start at the Sheepfold Turn.
Start at the Orchard Gate.

nodes.body: The Beacon Steps were ninety-one stone stairs cut into the ridge. A lantern bracket was fixed into the rock every fourth step. Ice had pulled three brackets right out of their holes. The seventh step from the bottom was gone. It left a knee-deep gap over loose stones. You could not use wheels here. Every crate had to be carried by hand. Wren stood at the bottom and looked up into the cloud. She had one afternoon to learn these stairs. The first thing she did was light a lantern. She put it on the lowest bracket, right where the wind hit hardest. She wanted to see what the ridge would do to it.

choices.label: Look at the loose brackets first.
Deal with the missing step.
Carry the crates up while it is dry.

nodes.body: The Sheepfold Turn was where the path had been moved. The hillside gave way there in February. The list named an old stretch of ground that walkers no longer used. It said nothing about the new line. Mr Ovens kept his ewes in the field the new path crossed. He had wired the gate shut with three tight turns of fence wire. A small note in pen said SHUT MEANS SHUT. Mr Ovens was gruff and exact. He had strong views about gates. But he was also the only person on the hill who knew where the village's old fuel stores were. He told Wren about three of them before she even asked.

choices.label: Look at the wired gate.
Walk the landslip and see what is left.
Go and find Mr Ovens.

nodes.body: The Orchard Gate was the bottom of the route, where twelve lanterns hung in old apple trees as the path left the lane. The branches were heavy with unpicked fruit, and the gate dragged a deep groove in the mud every time it moved. Last autumn somebody had hung the lanterns low enough for a walker to put a shoulder through one. The trees had grown since, and the same hooks now sat lower still.

choices.label: See to the dragging gate.
Sort out the low branches.
Deal with the fallen fruit.

nodes.body: Three brackets lay in the wet grass with their screws still in them, and the holes they had come out of were now wider than the screws. Frost had eaten the stone from the inside. A fourth bracket turned in its hole like a loose tooth, and the forecast pinned outside the shop promised more frost tonight. The wind tugged at Wren's collar as she knelt to look at the wreckage.

choices.label: Hunt down the jar of wall plugs.
Wire the brackets in instead.
Ask Dot Mallow what the shop has.

nodes.body: The seventh step from the bottom was gone, and the gap dropped a knee height onto scree. In afternoon light anyone could see it. After dusk it sat exactly where a tired walker would put a foot without thinking. Behind the shed there was one scaffold plank, four bricks and half a bag of cement that had been rained on and set hard.

choices.label: Hunt down the jar of wall plugs.
Wire the brackets in instead.
Ask Dot Mallow what the shop has.

nodes.body: Eighty lanterns weigh nothing on their own. But they weigh a great deal all together. The crates needed two hands each. The chalk note outside the shop said rain after four. Rafi could pull his bike trailer as far as the stile. But the last two hundred steps up the ridge were for whoever was carrying. The cloud was getting lower. The light had already gone a soft gold colour. This meant the afternoon was shorter than anyone had planned.

choices.label: Hunt down the jar of wall plugs.
Wire the brackets in instead.
Ask Dot Mallow what the shop has.

nodes.body: The gate onto the new path was wired shut with three turns of fencing wire and a note in blue biro that had been rained on twice: SHUT MEANS SHUT. The ewes stood in the top corner of the field with their backs to the wind, and the stile beside the gate had one plank missing and one plank green with moss.

choices.label: Work out where the lanterns go now.
Find something to hang the new ones on.
Make the turn obvious in the dark.

nodes.body: The old path stopped at a lip of raw earth. The hillside had come away there in February. Below it the ground was clay and torn heather roots. It was steep and soft and completely wrong for anyone walking in the dark. The list still had nine lanterns hung along the stretch that was no longer there.

choices.label: Work out where the lanterns go now.
Find something to hang the new ones on.
Make the turn obvious in the dark.

nodes.body: Mr Ovens was somewhere between the barn and the top field. He had said twice this year that the village treated his land like a hallway. He was the only person with a quad bike and a spare roll of wire. And he had never once let a walker come to harm on his hill. Wren found him mending a fence post. He moved with the same slow, careful steps he used for everything.

choices.label: Work out where the lanterns go now.
Find something to hang the new ones on.
Make the turn obvious in the dark.

nodes.body: The orchard gate ploughed a groove in the mud and took two hands and a shoulder to move. At two in the afternoon that was fine. At half past five, for someone with a pack on, it would be unkind. The hinge pin was worn to a shine, and the post itself was leaning downhill.

choices.label: Rehang the hooks where they belong.
Light the last stretch into the lane.
Take the twins up on their offer.

nodes.body: Last autumn someone had hung the orchard lanterns at eye height. They hung under branches heavy with fruit. A walker had put a shoulder through one. He got a face full of oil smell. The trees had grown since then. The fruit was still on them. The same hooks now sat even lower.

choices.label: Rehang the hooks where they belong.
Light the last stretch into the lane.
Take the twins up on their offer.

nodes.body: Windfalls lay three deep under the two old trees closest to the lane. The wasps in them were slow and cross in the cold. Nobody wanted to reach up into a tree above that. There was a barrow behind the wall. Clearing the fruit would use up about twenty minutes of the good light.

choices.label: Rehang the hooks where they belong.
Light the last stretch into the lane.
Take the twins up on their offer.

nodes.body: The jar of wall plugs was not on the shelf the list claimed it lived on. Mrs Trewin, called over from her crate, remembered it going up the steps last October and never coming down. That put it either in the heather at the top or in the back of a garage in the lane. The wind gusted across the shed yard, rattling a loose bracket on the step.

choices.label: Set the whole flight before the light goes.
Hang one lantern and watch it in the wind.
Go down and tell Mrs Trewin what the steps need.

nodes.body: There were two arm lengths of fence wire in the crate. There was also a way to hold a bracket that Mrs Trewin showed with her good hand. Twist it, tuck the sharp end down, and never leave a loop for a sleeve to catch. It held for a season. Everyone who had done it said so with a certain look. Wren practised on the loose fourth bracket until her fingers knew the steps.

choices.label: Measure the steps and write them up properly.
Set the whole flight before the light goes.
Hang one lantern and watch it in the wind.

nodes.body: The shop kept a drawer of odd bits under the till. Dot Mallow would find a use for any of it once you explained the job. She also had firm views about the ridge and owned a spare kettle. She had the only oil funnel in the village that did not leak. The shop bell rang as Wren pushed the door open. Dot looked up over her glasses. "Steps again, is it?"

choices.label: Go down and tell Mrs Trewin what the steps need.
Measure the steps and write them up properly.
Set the whole flight before the light goes.

nodes.body: The new path ran forty paces higher than the old one and turned twice where the old one had run straight. Nine lanterns in the old places would light a route that ended at a drop. The new line needed seven, and two of those had nothing to hang on. Wren stood at the turn, the wind pressing from the left, and counted the gaps out loud.

choices.label: Walk the new line carrying a crate.
Get the gate question settled properly.
Mark the drop above the slip.

nodes.body: There were no trees on the turn. There was no wall for a hundred steps either. The fence posts belonged to Mr Ovens. The shed could offer three thin bamboo sticks, a bundle of stakes for tomato plants, and a mallet with a split handle. Wren stood in the shed doorway and looked at the sad little pile. She tried to picture a tired walker finding it helpful in the dark.

choices.label: Leave the turn for the grown-ups and go back down.
Walk the new line carrying a crate.
Get the gate question settled properly.

nodes.body: A walker coming down in low cloud just followed the ground that looked most walked. That was still the old line heading straight for the landslip. No matter what else happened on this hill, the turning point had to be clear. It had to be clear at dusk to a tired person who had stopped reading the ground. The wind started to hum in the fence wire.

choices.label: Mark the drop above the slip.
Leave the turn for the grown-ups and go back down.
Walk the new line carrying a crate.

nodes.body: The right height for an orchard lantern was above the tallest walker with a pack. It also had to be below the branch that whipped in a gust. Finding that spot meant standing where the walkers walked and then looking up. You couldn't just stand where the ladder happened to be. Wren walked the path under the first tree. She raised a hand to where the lowest branch began its swing.

choices.label: Hang the orchard through before dusk.
Walk the orchard the way a walker would.
Take the spare lanterns up the ridge.

nodes.body: The last forty steps before the lane were the bit everyone forgot. The village lights were already easy to see from there. This was also where the ground was worst. There was a rut, a drain cover, and the corner where the orchard wall hid the turn. A walker who had been careful for an hour could trip right here without ever seeing it coming.

choices.label: Finish the orchard beautifully and stop there.
Hang the orchard through before dusk.
Walk the orchard the way a walker would.

nodes.body: Kit and Row were nine and had been standing at the gate for ten minutes waiting to be given something. They were entirely capable of carrying, counting and telling the truth about how many lanterns were left. They were not capable of being quiet or of being trusted with the mallet. "We saw you from the lane," Kit said. "What needs doing?"

choices.label: Take the spare lanterns up the ridge.
Finish the orchard beautifully and stop there.
Hang the orchard through before dusk.

nodes.body: The steps needed one lantern on every fourth bracket. That made twenty-two lanterns in all. Hanging from the bottom up meant carrying past everything already hung. Hanging from the top down meant walking back through the dark with nothing lit behind you. Wren stood at the foot of the steps with a crate by her feet. She tried to pick which type of hard this job was going to be.

choices.label: Get the paraffin sorted first.
Get more hands onto the ridge.
Walk the whole route once, end to end.

nodes.body: One lantern went up on the third bracket and just sat there swinging. The way it swung told you everything about how the other twenty-one would act. The wind on the steps came across the ridge, not up it. The list never said a word about that. The flame dipped once, held steady, and then bent nearly flat.

choices.label: Get ahead of the wind.
Send word up to the walking party.
Light the bottom of the route now.

nodes.body: There was a version of this afternoon where somebody walked back down and said plainly what the steps needed and how long that really took, and a version where nobody said it until dark. Mrs Trewin was at the hall with her wrist propped up and the kettle on. The hall door stood open, and the smell of tea drifted out into the yard.

choices.label: Get the paraffin sorted first.
Get more hands onto the ridge.
Walk the whole route once, end to end.

nodes.body: Carrying a crate along the new line was the only way to really learn it. It took eleven minutes at a working pace with the wind pushing from the left. The light on the hill had already gone amber. The cloud was coming down instead of lifting. Wren's arms ached from the crate, but her feet now knew every twist of the path.

choices.label: Get ahead of the wind.
Send word up to the walking party.
Light the bottom of the route now.

nodes.body: There was a huge gap between cutting the wire and being handed the wire. That gap would last a lot longer than tonight. Mr Ovens was at the barn until milking time. The lantern list had needed his field every fall for as long as it had been around. The sheep watched with calm eyes that never blinked while the question hung in the air.

choices.label: Get the paraffin sorted first.
Get more hands onto the ridge.
Walk the whole route once, end to end.

nodes.body: The lip of the landslip was the one spot on the whole route where a mistake cost more than a wet foot. Two lanterns and a cane would shout 'stop here' to someone who had stopped thinking. There were two spare lanterns only if the steps didn't end up needing them. The raw dirt edge was soft underfoot, so Wren stood well back.

choices.label: Get ahead of the wind.
Send word up to the walking party.
Light the bottom of the route now.

nodes.body: Twelve lanterns had to go in eleven trees. One of the trees took two. Each lantern was lit by a tiny flame on a stick. The orchard was the one spot on the route where the wind couldn't reach, yet somehow the matches still could. Wren went from trunk to trunk. The smell of lamp oil and wet grass mixed in the still air under the branches.

choices.label: Get the paraffin sorted first.
Get more hands onto the ridge.
Walk the whole route once, end to end.

nodes.body: Walking the orchard from the ridge end at a tired pace was the real test. It showed the lanterns from the same way a walker would see them, which was the opposite of how she'd hung them. From that side, two lanterns were hidden behind branches. One was stuck fully behind a tree trunk. Wren stopped and stared at the dark gaps. Nobody walking downhill would have seen them coming.

choices.label: Get ahead of the wind.
Send word up to the walking party.
Light the bottom of the route now.

nodes.body: The orchard needed twelve and the crate held sixteen, and four spare lanterns at the top of the ridge were worth a great deal more than four spare lanterns in a crate at the bottom of it. Carrying them up now cost the last of the easy light. The path climbed away from the shelter of the trees into a wind that was suddenly finding its voice.

choices.label: Get the paraffin sorted first.
Get more hands onto the ridge.
Walk the whole route once, end to end.

nodes.body: The shed door clicked shut. The new page was pinned to it. Every bracket was measured. The missing step was drawn to scale. The whole Beacon Steps were one honest record now. The lanterns would go up a week later on proper fixings. Someone else would carry. It was not the afternoon anyone had planned, but it was not nothing. The pencil went back into the tin. The door was shut on a job finished differently, but finished well.

ending.title: The Steps Get Their Own Page

nodes.body: The wire stayed on the gate. The new line stayed unlit. So at four, the rota was phoned round the village. Two adults walked the turn with head torches all evening. Nobody came to harm. Nobody thanked anybody. The list went back into its brown envelope, exactly as wrong as when it came out. Through the kitchen window, Wren watched the small circles of torchlight on the hill. She knew just where every lantern should have been.

The orchard ended up lit properly and prettily. The ridge above it did not. Walkers came down off the moor by torchlight. They met the lanterns only in the last five minutes of the way home. It looked like a welcome from the lane. It was meant to have been a route. The apples on the trees shone softly in the lantern glow. Nobody spoke of the long dark that came before.

The list said the paraffin lived in the hall cupboard, and the hall cupboard now held folding chairs. There were four litres in a can behind the shop, and the rest was wherever last autumn had left it. Eighty lanterns held rather more than four litres between them. The wind was getting up, and the clock on the hall wall said ten to four.

choices.label: Track down the rest of the paraffin.
Set up somewhere to fill them.
Go through the wicks before filling anything.

nodes.body: Only eleven people in the village had ever hung lanterns. About six of them were free on a Tuesday afternoon. Asking took time now but saved time later. The names list had not been right since the autumn before last. The hall clock ticked. Wren looked at the old list and thought about doors.

choices.label: Knock on the doors that used to say yes.
Catch people at the school gate.
Put the word out through the shop.

nodes.body: The first door was the one with the blue paint and the brass letterbox. Wren knocked, and old Mrs Kitto opened it before the echo had died. She had hung lanterns on this ridge for thirty years before her knees gave out, and she was holding a tin of boiled sweets and a list of her own. "I've been waiting," she said, and she was already putting on her coat.

choices.label: Knock on the doors that used to say yes.

nodes.body: Nobody had walked the full route today. The list showed a route that had changed in two places since it was written. Forty minutes of walking would answer more questions than an hour of guessing in the shed. The ridge path rolled out ahead, pale and stony, waiting to be checked.

choices.label: Walk the route with the list and a pencil.
Find the dark gaps between lanterns.
Look at what the rain has made of the ground.

nodes.body: The wind that came across the ridge at two was now bending the ash tree by the hall. Paper lanterns and wind had a long and costly past in this village. The shed held a box of storm shades. They fitted less than half the lanterns. Through the dusty window, the ash tree swayed like something under water.

choices.label: Track down the rest of the paraffin.
Set up somewhere to fill them.
Go through the wicks before filling anything.

nodes.body: Priya Shah was bringing fourteen people down off the moor. She expected a lit ridge by half past five. There was one bar of signal at the top of the steps and none in the orchard. The message she needed was not one that said everything was fine. The phone in Wren's pocket showed one weak bar. The wind pushed hard against her back.

choices.label: Knock on the doors that used to say yes.
Catch people at the school gate.
Put the word out through the shop.

nodes.body: Lighting from the bottom up kept the finished work behind you all afternoon. It showed the walkers the best part last. It also meant that if something went wrong at five, the lit part was nearest the village, the phone and the kettle. The orchard gate stood open. The first lantern of the low route was already on its hook.

choices.label: Walk the route with the list and a pencil.
Find the dark gaps between lanterns.
Look at what the rain has made of the ground.

nodes.body: Four litres behind the shop, a half can in the church boiler room that might be paraffin and might be lamp oil, and a full can that Mrs Trewin swore went to the school for the harvest lanterns and never came back. Dot Mallow pointed at the boiler room with her chin. "Smell it before you pour it," she said. "Harry once put white spirit in the lanterns and nearly singed the vicar."

choices.label: Go to the school for the missing can.
Ration what there is across the route.
Ration what there is across the route.
Burn one for twenty minutes and watch it.

nodes.body: Wren remembered Mr Ovens talking about the old fuel store in the church gate. Inside, behind the hymn books, was a full can. A five-litre one with a label in his writing: LANTERNS. She carried it back to the shed. The short supply problem suddenly looked much less worrying.

choices.label: Ration what there is across the route.

nodes.body: Filling eighty lanterns needed a funnel, a rag, a flat space, and a firm rule about where the full ones go. Doing it off a tailgate in the wind was how a village ended up with fuel down the inside of every crate it owned. The shed bench was cluttered with old tins and a dried-up brush. But it was out of the wind and it was flat.

choices.label: Ask the village for anything that burns.
Ask the village for anything that burns.
Fill fast and get the crates moving.
Go to the school for the missing can.

nodes.body: Wren remembered the second shop Mr Ovens talked about. It was a camping lamp in the chapel vestry. She fetched it, and the vicar pushed a box of night-light candles into her hands too. The pile of borrowed things on the bench was suddenly useful.

choices.label: Ask the village for anything that burns.

nodes.body: A wick that had sat in a shed for a year burned for twenty minutes. Then it went out sulking. There were two boxes of new wick in the drawer. They were cut to the wrong length. Trimming eighty of them was an hour of work nobody had. Half of them did not even need trimming. Wren pulled one of the old wicks out. She rubbed it between her fingers. It felt dry and smelled faintly of mouse.

choices.label: Ration what there is across the route.
Burn one for twenty minutes and watch it.
Ask the village for anything that burns.

nodes.body: The names column was three years out of date and read like a map of who had moved away. Four of the doors were still the right doors, and two of those opened onto somebody who had been waiting a long while to be asked again. Wren stood on the first doorstep, the list folded in her pocket, and raised a hand to knock.

choices.label: Split whoever comes into teams.
Show the new ones how a bracket holds.
Bring Mr Ovens in properly.

nodes.body: The school gate at half past three held more of the village than anywhere else all week. Nobody standing there was in a hurry for the next ten minutes. Parents in coats and children with book bags filled the pavement. A low hum of chatter filled the air. Wren spotted Kit and Row's mum near the front and headed straight for her.

choices.label: Give the twins a job that is really theirs.
Ask everybody and sort it out when they arrive.
Split whoever comes into teams.

nodes.body: Anything said across the counter at the shop was in eleven kitchens by teatime, and the version that arrived was the version Dot Mallow repeated, so the wording mattered a good deal more than the asking. The shop bell jangled, and Dot looked up from the till with the expression of someone who already knew there was a lantern emergency.

choices.label: Show the new ones how a bracket holds.
Bring Mr Ovens in properly.
Give the twins a job that is really theirs.

nodes.body: The list and the ground did not match in nine places. Only walking the route found the mistakes. The whole walk took thirty-eight minutes at a working pace. It took even longer with a crate. A pencil beat a memory every single time. Wren walked with the clipboard against her chest. She marked the page everywhere the path had changed.

choices.label: Respace the lanterns for the real path.
Make the drop above the slip safe.
Mark the turns with something better than light.

nodes.body: A lit route was not eighty lanterns. It was eighty gaps. The gap that mattered was the one where a walker could not see the next light. There were three gaps like that on this hill. None of them were marked. Wren stood at the first gap and looked back. The last lantern was a tiny yellow smudge. It was barely visible through the grey afternoon light.

choices.label: Find the sheltered hanging points.
Finish the survey properly before hanging anything.
Respace the lanterns for the real path.

nodes.body: The clay above the sheepfold turn was already greasy, and the forecast promised more after four. A lantern that showed a walker the wrong side of that slope was worse than no lantern there at all. Wren put a foot on the clay and felt it slide. A walker in the dark would have no chance of keeping upright here.

choices.label: Make the drop above the slip safe.
Mark the turns with something better than light.
Find the sheltered hanging points.

nodes.body: The school kitchen door stayed open until four. The caretaker knew exactly where the harvest lanterns went. He also knew what came back with them. The walk home with a full can was uphill and took both hands. The caretaker was a patient man called Mr Finch. He was already holding the can out when Wren reached the door. "Mrs Trewin phoned ahead," he said. "I've been expecting you since Tuesday."

choices.label: Run a filling line with the twins.
Fit the storm shades to the filled ones.
Get the filled crates to the top first.

nodes.body: Four litres would fill about fifty lanterns properly. Or it would fill eighty poorly. A badly filled lantern did not fail at seven in the evening. It failed at ten past five with the whole village watching the ridge. Wren lined up the first row of lanterns on the bench. She measured the paraffin with a steady hand and a kitchen measuring jug.

choices.label: Hold a reserve back at the hall.
Run a filling line with the twins.
Fit the storm shades to the filled ones.

nodes.body: One filled lantern on the shed step with a watch beside it answered the only question that really mattered. Would the thing burn from now until the walkers were down? It cost twenty minutes to find out. It cost rather more not to. The flame caught and settled into a steady yellow glow. The watch on the step began its slow counting.

choices.label: Get the filled crates to the top first.
Hold a reserve back at the hall.
Run a filling line with the twins.

nodes.body: There were storm lanterns from the pub. The chapel and three kitchens gave a camping lamp and a box of stubby candles in jam jars. None of them matched the route. But all of them made light. Wren stacked the borrowed things on the shed bench. Brass, glass, tin and wax. Every one of them could burn through an October evening.

choices.label: Fit the storm shades to the filled ones.
Get the filled crates to the top first.
Hold a reserve back at the hall.

nodes.body: Two on the steps, two in the orchard, one on the turn and one running between them. That was a plan. Six people all starting at the shed and talking was not. The difference was whoever spoke the first sentence. Wren looked at the faces gathered in the shed yard and took a breath.

choices.label: Write the rota where people can see it.
Set up a runner between the two ends.
Get the kettle going at the hall.

nodes.body: Everyone who had never hung a lantern did the first one badly and the second one well. The ten minutes spent teaching that were the cheapest of the whole afternoon. Wren took a bracket and a lantern. She walked through the steps slowly: hook, twist, settle, check. The new helpers watched. Their hands copied the moves in the air.

choices.label: Put Mrs Trewin where she can see the ridge.
Write the rota where people can see it.
Set up a runner between the two ends.

nodes.body: A quad bike carried four crates to the top of the ridge in the time a person carried one, and the price of asking was standing in a yard being told about gates for five minutes first, with your hands behind your back. Mr Ovens leaned on the quad's handlebars and looked at Wren. "Right then," he said. "The gate. Let's talk about the gate."

choices.label: Get the kettle going at the hall.
Put Mrs Trewin where she can see the ridge.
Write the rota where people can see it.

nodes.body: Kit and Row would do a dull job well for an hour if it was really theirs. If someone made it up to keep them busy, they would do it badly for four minutes. There was just one job on this route that fit them. Wren looked at the two of them, bouncing a little on their toes, and decided.

choices.label: Set up a runner between the two ends.
Get the kettle going at the hall.
Put Mrs Trewin where she can see the ridge.

nodes.body: The list spaced them out evenly, but the ground did not want them that way. It wanted them at the turns, at the drop, and at the two spots where the path looked like it went somewhere it did not. Wren stood back from the new plan, a pencil behind her ear, and looked at the ridge with fresh eyes. The lanterns would go where the hill asked for them.

choices.label: Hang the top section to the new plan.
Walk it in the half dark and look.
Keep four lanterns for whatever is wrong.

nodes.body: Two lanterns, a cane and a length of tape would say stop here in a way a tired person read without thinking about it, and every one of those lanterns came out of the count the top of the route was relying on. The raw edge of the landslip was dark with damp, and the wind funnelled up it in a low, constant moan.

choices.label: Get a light onto the sheepfold gate.
Hang the top section to the new plan.
Walk it in the half dark and look.

nodes.body: Paint on a stone lasts longer than any lantern, and the village had half a tin of white gate paint in the shed. The fight about painting stones on a hill had been going on since long before Mrs Trewin took the list. Wren pried the lid off the tin. The paint inside was still good and still white. It smelled of the shed and every argument ever had there.

choices.label: Keep four lanterns for whatever is wrong.
Get a light onto the sheepfold gate.
Hang the top section to the new plan.

nodes.body: The wind came across the ridge, not up it. This made the sheltered side of every wall, post, and thorn on the route worth a lantern that would still burn at seven. Wren crouched behind a low drystone wall and felt the wind pass clean over her head. Here, in this pocket of still air, a lantern would burn all night.

choices.label: Walk it in the half dark and look.
Keep four lanterns for whatever is wrong.
Get a light onto the sheepfold gate.

nodes.body: A can went over on the shed step and took the afternoon with it. The smell was everywhere, sharp and slick. The sand went down, the crate had to be washed out twice, and by the time the yard was safe the light was going. The ridge would be walked with head torches tonight, and the lanterns would go up on Saturday.

Nine people showed up at ten past four and stood in the shed asking what to do while the light faded. By the time there was a list of who was doing what, the ridge had turned blue. The lanterns went up by torchlight, all crooked. Everyone said it was lovely to see everyone out. Dot Mallow said it was the nicest mess she had seen in years.

The survey was done at ten past five. It was honest, complete, and truly useful, but the hill was not lit. That evening the list was rewritten at the kitchen table into something true. The lanterns would go up on Saturday in daylight, with everyone knowing where they belonged. Wren looked at the new page and thought: this is how it should always have been.

ending.title: A Very Good Map of a Dark Hill

nodes.body: One person filled, one wiped, one carried. The line moved at the speed of the slowest job, and that was always the wiping. Kit and Row would hold that line for as long as somebody kept counting out loud. "Thirty-seven," Row shouted. Kit wiped the neck of the next lantern with a rag already dark with paraffin.

choices.label: Plan for the ones that go out.
Get the tapers and matches sorted.
Count what is actually lit.

nodes.body: The storm shades fit forty of the eighty lanterns. They went on easily before a lantern was hung, but horribly after, in the wind. The ones without shades had to hang where the ridge sheltered them. That meant a whole new plan for the top half. Wren held a glass shade up to the light. It was smeared from last year but in one piece. It would stop a gust from killing a flame.

choices.label: Get a message to Priya about the timing.
Fill fifty properly and leave the rest empty.
Plan for the ones that go out.

nodes.body: The top of the route was the furthest from the shed. It was the last place anyone wanted to be carrying at five o'clock. The argument for doing it first got harder to make with every ten minutes that passed. The crates were ready. The light was going. The path up the ridge looked very long.

choices.label: Get the tapers and matches sorted.
Count what is actually lit.
Get a message to Priya about the timing.

nodes.body: Six filled lanterns and a can kept at the hall. They were either the most sensible thing anyone did today, or they were six lanterns of ridge left dark. Which one it turned out to be depended on what went wrong later. The hall floor was cool and dim. The six lanterns sat in a neat row against the wall, waiting.

choices.label: Fill fifty properly and leave the rest empty.
Plan for the ones that go out.
Get the tapers and matches sorted.

nodes.body: A rota on a paper in a pocket was just a guess. A rota chalked on the shed door was real. The shed door held soft chalk marks from every fall, right back to when the lamps were tin. Wren took up the chalk. The end was worn flat from years of use. She began to write.

choices.label: Have somebody check the top pair.
Keep the top half with the team that knows it.
Send two people up for the signal.

nodes.body: You could not see the orchard from the top of the steps. One end could not hear the other. A runner who knew both ends was worth more than a phone with no signal. It was also the coldest job on the hill, and nobody ever picked it. The wind was getting up. The run between the two ends now felt much longer than it had at two.

choices.label: Get everyone off the hill by six.
Let the village finish it however it likes.
Let the village finish it however it likes.
Have somebody check the top pair.

nodes.body: Old Mrs Kitto, who had been a lantern keeper longer than anyone, was already there, directing three volunteers with the calm authority of someone who had done this thirty times. She caught Wren's eye and nodded. "Go on," she said. "I've got this end. Get them all down safe." Wren turned and ran for the steps.

choices.label: Get everyone off the hill by six.

nodes.body: A kettle at the hall at half past four was not a treat. It stopped six people going home at five. Mrs Trewin could run it one handed, as long as someone else fetched the water. The big steel kettle was already on the stove. The hall was starting to smell of tea and something warm.

choices.label: Keep the top half with the team that knows it.
Send two people up for the signal.
Get everyone off the hill by six.

nodes.body: She could not carry and she could not climb, but she could stand on the hall steps, look at the ridge, and point out the wrong lamp from four hundred steps away. This was the one skill the others on the hill did not have. Mrs Trewin sat down in a chair by the hall door. Her hurt wrist lay in her lap and her eyes were already fixed on the ridge line.

choices.label: Let the village finish it however it likes.
Have somebody check the top pair.
Keep the top half with the team that knows it.

nodes.body: The top part needed nineteen lamps with the new spacing. The crate that made it to the stile held just sixteen. So someone had to go back down the steps, or the last three spots would stay dark. The wind was stronger up here. The lamps swung as soon as they touched the hooks.

choices.label: Close the last gap on the ridge.
Go back for the two that blew out.
Go up and meet the party at the top.

nodes.body: By half past four the ridge was dark enough to test. Walking it downhill in that light was the only way to see it as the walkers would. Two things that had looked fine at two were gone when seen from above. The whole path felt odd coming down. The light was behind you and the dark was where you were going.

choices.label: Hold the bottom and let them come down.
Leave the shoulder and light everything else.
Close the last gap on the ridge.

nodes.body: Every fall, something broke at the last minute that no one saw coming. Four spare lamps in a bag at the top of the steps was the cheapest help this town had ever bought. The cloth bag sat at Wren's feet. The lamps inside it clinked softly when the wind moved.

choices.label: Go back for the two that blew out.
Go up and meet the party at the top.
Hold the bottom and let them come down.

nodes.body: The new gate was the one spot where a walker had to do something, not just keep walking. Doing something in the dark without a light was where every fight about this path had started. The wire still held the gate shut. The note was still there, damp but easy to read.

choices.label: Leave the shoulder and light everything else.
Close the last gap on the ridge.
Go back for the two that blew out.

nodes.body: Some of the lamps would go out. This was why the word ROUND was written three times on the side of the list. Someone had to walk the whole path again at seven, with a light in a jar. Wren looked at the ridge. The tiny flames already fought the wind and she knew the first ones that would fail.

choices.label: Wait at the top of the steps.
Get the phone up to the signal.
Walk the route counting what is lit.

nodes.body: There were two boxes of matches, one of them damp, and a bundle of sticks Mrs Trewin had cut from a broom handle years ago. Lighting eighty lanterns in wind was not a match job. It was a taper job, and that meant about forty minutes of standing still. Wren tested a taper. The dry wood caught at once and burned with a steady, patient flame.

choices.label: Fetch the head torches from the hall.
Go up the ridge to meet them.
Get the hall ready for fourteen cold people.

nodes.body: The only real count was one a person had walked and marked. The list had a tally box at the bottom. People had filled it in with pencil each fall, since long before any of them were born. Wren looked at the box and its layers of old pencil marks. Some were so faded they were nearly gone, but others from last year were still dark and sharp.

choices.label: Ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.
Take a taper to the shoulder.
Hold the plan and trust the route.

nodes.body: The party was coming down the hill no matter what. So the best note was a number and a time, not a vow. The signal at the top of the steps held for about a minute and then went away. Wren held the phone up and watched the one bar blink. She put the short text together in her head before she typed it.

choices.label: Wait at the top of the steps.
Get the phone up to the signal.
Walk the route counting what is lit.

nodes.body: The two highest lanterns hung where the walkers saw them first from the moor. No one walked back to check them, and they caught the worst wind with the least shelter on the route. Wren looked up. The lanterns were small and brave against the grey sky. She wondered if they were still burning.

choices.label: Fetch the head torches from the hall.
Go up the ridge to meet them.
Get the hall ready for fourteen cold people.

nodes.body: The steps team learned the route in one afternoon. They knew exactly which brackets turned in their holes. Giving all that away at five o'clock to new people cost more than fresh legs were worth. The team looked at Wren, waiting. Their hands still held the motions they had practised.

choices.label: Ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.
Ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.
Take a taper to the shoulder.
Hold the plan and trust the route.

nodes.body: Old Mrs Kitto had known Mr Ovens for forty years. She picked up the phone in the hall and spoke five words into it. Two minutes later, the quad's engine started in his yard.

choices.label: Ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.

nodes.body: The phone signal at the top of the steps was one bar. One person alone up there at dusk was the reason the rota rule about pairs was written. It was in capital letters, twice. Wren looked at the list, then the darkening sky. Then she looked at the faces of the people who must go up.

choices.label: Wait at the top of the steps.
Get the phone up to the signal.
Walk the route counting what is lit.

nodes.body: The most important rule was not about lanterns. Everyone who went up had to come down and be counted before the walkers arrived. The counting was the part people forgot on a good day. The names were on the chalk board, and they had to be checked off one by one.

choices.label: Fetch the head torches from the hall.
Go up the ridge to meet them.
Get the hall ready for fourteen cold people.

nodes.body: The gap from the top of the steps to the first ridge lantern was ninety paces of nothing at all. It was the part of the route a walker met first, and met when tired. Wren stood at the top step and looked across the open stretch. In the half-light it looked like the surface of the moon.

choices.label: Ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.
Take a taper to the shoulder.
Hold the plan and trust the route.

nodes.body: Two lanterns on the bare shoulder had gone out once already. They would do it again. The real question was whether to stand with them or move them somewhere the wind was not. The wind on the shoulder was a solid, pushing thing. The dead lanterns swung on their hooks like bells with no tongues.

choices.label: Wait at the top of the steps.
Get the phone up to the signal.
Walk the route counting what is lit.

nodes.body: Walking up to meet fourteen people off the moor turned a lit route into a welcome. It meant being out on the hill in the dark on purpose, not by accident. That was a different thing to explain afterwards. The path ahead was unlit. The wind on the open moor was a different creature from the wind on the ridge.

choices.label: Fetch the head torches from the hall.
Go up the ridge to meet them.
Get the hall ready for fourteen cold people.

nodes.body: Standing at the orchard gate with a lamp and letting the hill do its own work was the harder choice and the one the rota was written around. The route was either good enough now or it was not. Wren stood still, the lamp steady in her hand, and watched the ridge and waited.

choices.label: Ask Mr Ovens for the quad bike.

Hold the plan and trust the route.

nodes.body: Fifty went up filled properly and thirty stayed in the crate. The moon did more work than anyone expected. The walkers came down easily. They never knew there had been a plan at all. The tally box got a fifty in it with a note beside it about the missing can. The ridge was not full, but it was enough. The darkness between the lanterns was gentle rather than frightening.

ending.title: Fifty Lanterns and a Rising Moon

nodes.body: The ridge got lit by fourteen people who mostly did not know each other at two o'clock. Because of that, half the lanterns hung at slightly wrong heights. The list went back in the envelope with eleven new names in the column. One of them was underlined. The village had turned up in its messy, unpractised way. The hill was brighter than it had been in years.

The route was lit end to end except for one stretch on the shoulder. That stretch swallowed two lanterns twice over. The walkers came down chattering and never noticed the dark they crossed. The tally box said seventy-eight. The note beside it said shoulder, again. The gap was still there and would still be there next year, but tonight it had not mattered.

Half past five went by. The ridge was lit and nobody was on it. The moor above was a flat grey where fourteen people should be. Ten minutes late off a moor meant nothing at all. Forty minutes meant something. The wind was colder now, and the lanterns on the steps were all still burning. Their small flames were steady in the dusk.

choices.label: Move the six to the leeward side.
Send a pair up with the spare bag.
Put a lamp at the orchard corner.

nodes.body: There was one bar at the top step. A message Priya had sent twenty minutes ago arrived all at once. They were down off the tops. One of them had turned an ankle. They were moving slower than the light was going. Wren read the message twice. The phone screen was harsh and bright in the growing dark.

choices.label: Set a relay along the lit stretch.
Keep the signal watch at the top step.
Get help to the walker with the ankle.

nodes.body: Seventy-one lanterns were lit. Six were out and three were never hung. The six that were out all sat within two hundred paces on the open part of the hill where the wind came across. Wren walked the count slowly. She touched each bracket. The tally grew in her head like a song.

choices.label: Wait at the sheepfold gate with a light.
Wait at the sheepfold gate with a light.
Finish the tally and write it down.
Go round once more with the taper.

nodes.body: Wren had tested the wind on the steps earlier. She knew just where to stand so the flame would not flicker. She cupped her hand around the lantern at the gate. It burned as steady as it would in the shed.

choices.label: Wait at the sheepfold gate with a light.

nodes.body: The hall cupboard held four head torches. Two of them had batteries in. This was the sort of fact the list was meant to hold. It did not say it anywhere. Wren pulled the cupboard open. She shone one of the working torches at the ceiling. The beam was weak, but it was light.

choices.label: Stand where you are and let the ridge do its work.
Get them down before the weather closes in.
Count them in and check the tally.

nodes.body: Going up meant walking away from every light on the path. You went into the part of the hill that never had a lantern. It meant someone at the bottom had to know just where you went and when. The dark past the last lantern was total. The wind on the open moor had a voice in it.

choices.label: Rewrite the list while it is all still fresh.
Stay on the shoulder and watch what the wind does.
Give the turn the last two lanterns.
Give the turn the last two lanterns.

nodes.body: Wren remembered the wind test from earlier: how it came across, not up. She moved the last two lanterns into the lee of a low wall, and they caught and held immediately. The turn was lit, and the steps would be too. She turned back toward the hall, the list crisp in her pocket, and started writing the new version in her head.

choices.label: Rewrite the list while it is all still fresh.

nodes.body: The hall had a kettle. It had a heater that worked. It had the wrong number of chairs. Fourteen people off a moor at six on an October night wanted all three more than a pretty ridge. The heater clanked and hissed. The kettle was already starting to sing.

choices.label: Move the six to the leeward side.
Send a pair up with the spare bag.
Put a lamp at the orchard corner.

nodes.body: The quad could climb the track to the sheepfold turn in four minutes. It had a person and a bag on the back. Asking for it twice in one afternoon was a different kind of ask than the first. The quad was parked by the barn. Its engine was still warm from the last run. Mr Ovens was wiping his hands on a rag.

choices.label: Set a relay along the lit stretch.
Keep the signal watch at the top step.
Get help to the walker with the ankle.

nodes.body: Six lanterns out in one stretch was not bad luck. It was the wind finding the one spot no one had thought hard enough about. Lighting them again where they hung meant doing it all over in twenty minutes. Wren held the taper in its jar. The flame danced behind the glass. She looked at the dark part of the shoulder.

choices.label: Wait at the sheepfold gate with a light.
Finish the tally and write it down.
Go round once more with the taper.

nodes.body: The route was lit, the rota was written, and the tally was counted. The urge now was to keep changing things. In a version of this evening, the best thing anyone could do was nothing at all. Wren stood still on the ridge path. The lit line ran away below her. She let the hill be.

choices.label: Stand where you are and let the ridge do its work.
Get them down before the weather closes in.
Count them in and check the tally.

nodes.body: Moving a lantern in the dark meant unhooking, carrying and rehanging with cold hands, and the leeward line was nine paces off the path, which was nine paces of light the walkers would not get. Wren worked methodically, moving each lantern to the sheltered side of the wall, where the wind passed over and left the flame alone.

choices.label: Walk them down and get the door open.
See them safely round the turn.
Get the top pair lit before they clear the tops.

nodes.body: Four spare lanterns, a taper, a jar and two people who knew the shoulder could close the dark stretch in twelve minutes, and the pair had to be back down before the party reached the turn. Wren handed the bag to the two volunteers and pointed up the hill. "You know where to go. Be back in twelve."

choices.label: Send the quad up with the last crate.
Fill in the tally box and hang the list back up.
Hand the list back to Mrs Trewin.

nodes.body: The orchard corner was where the wall hid the turn. A tired group with a hurt ankle would make its one mistake of the night there. A storm lantern on the gatepost fixed it for good. Wren set the lantern on the post. Its light spilled over the rough ground and the drain grate. It made the risky corner easy to see.

choices.label: Write down what the list should have said.
Light what is left after they are down.
Leave the shoulder to the wind and go down.

nodes.body: Three people spaced along the lit stretch could pass a message from the moor to the hall in under two minutes without any signal at all, and it used the three people who were going to walk up anyway. The relay formed in the dusk, voices carrying the message from one pool of lantern light to the next: "Ankle. Slow. Coming."

choices.label: Walk them down and get the door open.
See them safely round the turn.
Get the top pair lit before they clear the tops.

nodes.body: One pair stood on the top step. They held the phone at just the right angle. That was how the village heard what was going on on the moor. It meant twenty minutes of standing still in the wind. They seemed to do nothing. The watchers held the phone out into the wind and turned it slowly. The one bar of signal held steady.

choices.label: Send the quad up with the last crate.
Fill in the tally box and hang the list back up.
Hand the list back to Mrs Trewin.

nodes.body: A turned ankle three hundred steps above the sheepfold gate needed help. It needed a shoulder to lean on, a light, and someone who stayed calm. The quad could meet them at the turn if the gate was open and someone was standing there. Wren shone the torch beam up the path. She looked for the first sign of movement on the dark hillside.

choices.label: Write down what the list should have said.
Light what is left after they are down.
Leave the shoulder to the wind and go down.

nodes.body: The gate was the pinch point of the whole evening. Fourteen people, one hurt, a wired hinge, and a field of ewes. Whoever stood there with a lamp decided how the next ten minutes went. The wire was off. The gate stood wide. Wren held the lantern high as the first walker came out of the dark.

choices.label: Walk them down and get the door open.
See them safely round the turn.
Get the top pair lit before they clear the tops.

nodes.body: The tally box wanted a number. The margin wanted the truth. The truth this year had a missing can, a gate, a landslip, and six lanterns that would not stay lit on the shoulder. Wren wrote the number first, seventy-eight, in clear pencil. Then she filled the margin with the facts the next autumn would need.

choices.label: Send the quad up with the last crate.
Fill in the tally box and hang the list back up.
Hand the list back to Mrs Trewin.

nodes.body: One more round of the whole route at ten to six. They had to relight whatever had gone out. It was the oldest rule on the list, written in the steadiest hand. Wren took the taper in its jar and began to walk. The flame was a small, steady star against the huge darkness of the hill.

choices.label: Write down what the list should have said.
Light what is left after they are down.
Leave the shoulder to the wind and go down.

nodes.body: The party came off the moor into a line of lights. The lights ran unbroken from the top of the steps to the orchard gate. Fourteen people walked down talking about the view. Nothing big happened anywhere on the hill. That was what the list had been trying to do since 1953. The ridge held its light. The light held the walkers. Somewhere in the village hall, a kettle was already boiling.

The last of the party reached the orchard gate at twenty-five past six. They were ten minutes ahead of the rain. The lanterns were still burning behind them all the way up the hill. Priya counted fourteen twice and then stopped counting. The first drops of rain began to fall just as the hall door closed. Behind them, the ridge was still a line of warm yellow lights in the dark.

Seventy-eight lights were lit. Fourteen walkers were in. Six people were off the hill. All of it went into the tally box in pencil before anyone sat down. It was the first year in three that the numbers on the page and the numbers on the hill were the same. Wren looked at the tally and saw the neat pencil marks. She felt the deep, quiet joy of a count that added up.

The list was rewritten on the hall table while the mud was still on everyone. The new one had the landslip in it, and the gate, and the shoulder. And it had eleven names that were true. Mrs Trewin signed the bottom with her left hand. It was barely easy to read, but it was there. The old list went into the envelope for the last time, and the new one hung on its nail, ready for next year.

Twenty minutes on the shoulder with a taper taught more about that stretch than nine autumns of hanging lanterns on it. The gusts came in threes across the ridge. Nothing hung on the path side could survive the second gust. The walk went on without her. The notebook filled up with the kind of knowledge that only came from standing still in the dark and paying close attention.

ending.title: What the Wind Does on the Shoulder

nodes.body: The turn was lit. The top of the steps was not. The party came down the steps in the dark with one head torch between fourteen people. Nobody fell and everybody noticed. The steps got talked about at the hall in the voice the village kept for near misses. If someone had known how the wind really moved across those top steps, those last two lanterns might have been enough.

ending.title: Two Lanterns Short at the Steps

nodes.body: Fourteen people, one strapped ankle, and six lantern keepers came through the hall door at twenty to seven. They came into a room with a working radiator and the wrong number of chairs. Behind them, the ridge was still burning end to end in the rain. The hall filled with the smell of wet wool and tea. Someone found an extra chair. The ankle was propped up on a crate that had held lanterns two hours ago.

The new line above the sheepfold did just what it was rehung to do. Fourteen people walked the turn. Not one of them drifted onto the old ground above the slip. Not one of them noticed there had ever been a choice to make there. The lanterns guided them around the danger so smoothly that the danger might as well not have been there. That was the whole point.

From the moor the ridge showed as a line of small warm dots a mile off. Priya said later that the group had stopped walking when they came over the last rise and saw it. That was the whole point of the lanterns, and it was not written down anywhere on the list. The walkers stood in the dark, a mile from home, and looked at the lights put there for them.

ending.title: A Ridge You Could See From the Moor

nodes.body: The quad took the last crate and two people to the sheepfold turn in four minutes. The gate stood open with a lamp on the post. Mr Ovens stood beside it in the rain telling everyone this was his field. The walkers thanked him, and he nodded. The gate swung shut behind the last of them with the soft click of a job done right.

The tally box got its number, the margin got four lines of truth about the shoulder, and the clipboard went back on its nail in the shed with the pencil on the string. Next autumn would start from a page that was not lying. The shed door closed, and the list hung in the dark, ready for whoever needed it next.

The list came back with a mended fixing and a new name in the column. A section was rewritten and page two had a smear of paraffin in the corner. Mrs Trewin read it with her wrist on the table and said only that it would do. Coming from her, that was a great deal. She looked up at Wren. Her eyes were the same colour as the ridge in autumn, and she nodded once.

ending.title: Handed Back Better Than It Came

nodes.body: The evening ended with the ridge half lit and a page of notes that nobody asked for. It told where the path really went, what the wind did, which brackets turned, and how long the steps took with a crate. It was the most useful thing written about this hill in years and it had lit nothing at all tonight. But it would light something next year, and the year after that.

ending.title: The Page That Should Have Been There

nodes.body: The party got home before the ridge was finished. The last eleven lanterns went up at seven in the rain for nobody. They burned over an empty hill until the wind took three at nine. Dot Mallow was closing up the shop. She looked up at the ridge, saw the small brave lights, and thought: someone cared enough to finish.

The shoulder went dark for the third time and stayed dark. Fourteen people crossed two hundred paces of it on one head torch with the rain coming in sideways. Everyone got down. Nobody was hurt. Nobody said the ridge was lit this year. The shoulder had won again. But the notes about why were already written down, and next year would be different.
